lessons.title: One operator, a few names
explanation: Nested expressions hide too much work in one tree node. `(a + b) * c` is a single plus-times tree. Three-address code names each result: `t1 = a + b` then `t2 = t1 * c`. Each instruction has one operator and a handful of operands. A later pass that wants to move or fold work rewrites those small instructions, not a tree it has to unpack.

The temporaries are the point. Once every subexpression has a name, you can copy `t1`, replace `t1`, or delete `t1` without walking children. Motion is cheap because the unit of motion is already small.
lessons.example: `x = (a + b) * (a + b)` becomes `t1 = a + b; t2 = a + b; t3 = t1 * t2; x = t3`. Two identical adds sit in the open. A later pass can see they are the same work.
lessons.whyItMatters: Optimizers move instructions, not parentheses. If the IR is still a nested tree, every rewrite re-implements lowering.

quiz.stem: Rewrite `(a + b) * c` into three-address instructions:
quiz.correctAnswer: `t1 = a + b` then `t2 = t1 * c`

distractors.text: Keep `(a + b) * c` as one nested instruction
distractors.rationale: That is still a tree node, not three-address.

distractors.text: `t1 = a + b * c` with both operators in one step
distractors.rationale: One operator per instruction; the multiply is a second step.

distractors.text: Emit a single fused machine opcode and stop
distractors.rationale: Three-address is still IR. Target opcodes come later.

quiz.correctExplanation: Name the add, then multiply that name. Each step has one operator.
objectiveIds: Rewrite a nested expression into three-address instructions with temporary names

quiz.stem: One operator and a few operands make later motion easy because:
quiz.correctAnswer: Each instruction is already a small unit a pass can move or replace

distractors.text: Nested trees are illegal after type checking
distractors.rationale: Trees are fine as a front-end form; they are just awkward to move.

distractors.text: The CPU only executes three-operand instructions
distractors.rationale: This is an IR shape, not a hardware rule.

distractors.text: Temporaries forbid any later rewrite of the program
distractors.rationale: Names exist so rewrites have something to grab.

quiz.correctExplanation: Small named units move. A nested tree makes every rewrite unpack children.
objectiveIds: Explain why one operator and a few operands make later motion easy

quiz.stem: In `t1 = a + b; t2 = t1 * c`, the name `t1` exists so that:
quiz.correctAnswer: The multiply can mention the add's result without nesting

distractors.text: The lexer can recover the original parentheses
distractors.rationale: Lexing is over. This is already three-address IR.

distractors.text: The add and multiply share one instruction slot
distractors.rationale: They are two instructions; the name is the wire between them.

distractors.text: A later pass must re-parse `a + b` from source
distractors.rationale: The point of the temporary is to stop re-parsing.

quiz.correctExplanation: The temporary is the result. Later instructions mention it, not a nested tree.
objectiveIds: Rewrite a nested expression into three-address instructions with temporary names

lessons.title: Temporaries later passes can move
explanation: Stanford CS143 treats three-address as the form later motion can actually rewrite. A nested source expression is a tree. Lowering names every interior result: `t1 = a + b`, `t2 = t1 * c`, `x = t2`. Each instruction carries one operator and a few operands. That is the unit a later pass copies, folds, or deletes.

CMU 15-411 puts the same cut at the start of IR: once names exist, control can be drawn as blocks and edges. `t1 = a + b` can live in an entry block and feed both sides of a branch. You do not have to keep the plus glued inside a source statement. The instruction is already a thing that can sit on an edge.

The alternative is to keep the tree and re-walk it in every pass. That works until a pass wants to hoist `a + b` above a branch or share it with another statement. Then the tree is in the way. Three-address pays the naming cost once so motion stays local.
lessons.example: `if (c) x = a + b; else x = 0;` lowers to `t1 = a + b` in the then-path, `t2 = 0` in the else-path, and `x` assigned from whichever name arrives. The add is one instruction, not a nested AST node stuck inside the `if`.
lessons.whyItMatters: Every later CFG, SSA, and fold pass assumes this grain. If you still have a tree, you are arguing with lowering, not optimizing.

quiz.stem: Trace `x = (a + b) * c` into three-address with temporaries:

distractors.text: `x = a + b * c` as a single three-operand instruction
distractors.rationale: That still hides two operators; the add needs its own name.

distractors.text: Leave `(a + b) * c` as one AST plus-times node
distractors.rationale: That is the tree you just lowered out of.

distractors.text: Emit the source characters `a`, `+`, `b` as three tokens
distractors.rationale: Tokens are a front-end object. This is already IR.

quiz.correctExplanation: Name the add, name the multiply, assign `x`. Each line is one operator.
objectiveIds: Rewrite a nested expression into three-address instructions with temporary names

quiz.stem: A pass that wants to hoist `a + b` out of a statement prefers three-address because:
quiz.correctAnswer: The add is already one named instruction it can pick up and move

distractors.text: Three-address forbids moving any instruction at all
distractors.rationale: The form exists so motion is local.

distractors.text: The source tree already has a unique name for every plus
distractors.rationale: Trees share structure; they do not name interior results as instructions.

distractors.text: Hoisting is a parser rewrite of the original parentheses
distractors.rationale: The parser is finished. Motion happens on IR.

quiz.correctExplanation: Small named units move. A nested plus inside a statement does not.
objectiveIds: Explain why one operator and a few operands make later motion easy

quiz.stem: `t1 = a + b` in an entry block that feeds two successors is useful because:
quiz.correctAnswer: Both successors can mention `t1` without recomputing the add

distractors.text: Each successor must re-parse `a + b` from the source file
distractors.rationale: The temporary already holds the result.

distractors.text: The add must be duplicated into every successor, always
distractors.rationale: Sharing the name is the point; duplication is a later choice.

distractors.text: Entry blocks are forbidden from holding arithmetic
distractors.rationale: Arithmetic is ordinary three-address; blocks just group it.

quiz.correctExplanation: The name travels on the edges. That is why one operator and a name beat a nested tree.
objectiveIds: Explain why one operator and a few operands make later motion easy

lessons.title: Straight line, not a soup
explanation: Control splits a three-address stream into basic blocks. A block is a straight-line sequence: one entry, one exit, no branch in the middle. Instructions inside run in order or not at all. The edges between blocks are the taken and not-taken paths, the loop back-edge, the merge after an `if`.

Stanford CS143 draws the CFG after three-address exists for a reason. `t1 = a + b` is an instruction you can put in a block. A branch that tests `c` is the block's exit. The then-block holds `t2 = t1`; the else-block holds `t3 = 0`; both edges land in a join. Without the split, 'move this add' has no place to move to.

Leaders start a block: the first instruction, a branch target, an instruction after a branch. Everything from a leader up to the next leader is one block. The graph is those blocks plus the successor edges. Later dataflow walks the graph, not the original source statements.
lessons.example: `t1 = a + b; if c goto L1; t3 = 0; goto L2; L1: t2 = t1; L2: ...` splits into an entry block ending at the branch, a then-block, an else-block, and a join. Four blocks, not one soup of labels.
lessons.whyItMatters: Every global rewrite names blocks and edges. If you still see a linear dump of gotos, you will miss the join.

quiz.stem: A basic block is:
quiz.correctAnswer: A straight-line sequence with one entry and one exit

distractors.text: Any run of three-address code including a mid-block branch
distractors.rationale: A branch in the middle splits the block at that exit.

distractors.text: The entire function treated as a single instruction list
distractors.rationale: Joins and branches cut the list into blocks.

distractors.text: A source-level statement, including a nested `if`
distractors.rationale: The CFG is built on three-address, not on source statements.

quiz.correctExplanation: One entry, one exit, straight line. That is the definition later passes use.
objectiveIds: Identify a basic block as a straight-line sequence with one entry and one exit

quiz.stem: Split `t1 = a + b; if c goto T; t3 = 0; goto J; T: t2 = t1; J: x = ...` into blocks:
quiz.correctAnswer: Entry ending at the branch, then-block, else-block, and a join

distractors.text: One block containing every instruction and both labels
distractors.rationale: Labels and branches are the cuts; they start and end blocks.

distractors.text: A separate block for each three-address operator, no edges
distractors.rationale: Straight-line runs stay together; edges connect the runs.

distractors.text: Keep the original AST `if` as a single tree node
distractors.rationale: The CFG is three-address blocks, not the source tree.

quiz.correctExplanation: Leaders at the start, the branch target, and the fall-through. Edges carry the join.
objectiveIds: Split three-address code into basic blocks and the edges between them

quiz.stem: An instruction after a conditional branch belongs in:
quiz.correctAnswer: A new block, because the branch was the previous block's exit

distractors.text: The same block, appended after the branch
distractors.rationale: Nothing in a block runs after its exit.

distractors.text: No block, because fall-through is not an edge
distractors.rationale: Fall-through is an edge to the next leader.

distractors.text: The lexer token stream, which still owns control
distractors.rationale: Lexing is over. This is already three-address IR.

quiz.correctExplanation: The branch exits. The next instruction is a leader. That is how edges appear.
objectiveIds: Identify a basic block as a straight-line sequence with one entry and one exit

lessons.title: Each name is written once
explanation: Assignments that reuse a name hide which write a later use actually reads. Three-address still allows `x = 1; x = 2; return x`. Static single assignment gives each write a fresh name: `x1 = 1; x2 = 2`. Each name is defined exactly once. A use of `x2` has one definition, not a search through earlier stores to `x`.

LLVM's Language Reference treats that single definition as the IR's data contract. Use-def is then a graph: each use points at one instruction. Constant propagation, copy replacement, and dead-name deletion become walks of that graph instead of a hunt through every assignment of `x`.

Joins still need a story. When `x` is assigned on two incoming paths, SSA inserts a merge: `x3 = φ(x1, x2)`. The φ is a new definition, so `x3` is still written once. φ-nodes are how SSA names that join. Here the rule is the names: one write per name, even at a merge.
lessons.example: `x = 1; if (c) x = 2; return x;` in three-address reassigns `x`. In SSA it is `x1 = 1; x2 = 2; x3 = φ(x1, x2); return x3`. The return uses one name, defined once.
lessons.whyItMatters: If a name has two writers, every pass re-solves reaching definitions. SSA pays that cost once, as renaming.

quiz.stem: Rewrite `x = 1; x = x + y; z = x` so each name is defined once:

distractors.text: Keep `x = 1; x = x + y; z = x` and mark `x` as SSA anyway
distractors.rationale: Reassignment of `x` is exactly what SSA forbids.

distractors.text: `x1 = 1; x1 = x1 + y; z = x1` with one name written twice
distractors.rationale: The second write must be a new name.

distractors.text: Collapse everything to the source identifiers `x` and `z`
distractors.rationale: Source names are not SSA names; each write needs a version.

quiz.correctExplanation: Fresh name per write. Uses mention the version they read.
objectiveIds: Rewrite assignments so each name is defined exactly once

quiz.stem: A single definition per name turns use-def into a graph walk because:
quiz.correctAnswer: Each use has exactly one defining instruction to follow

distractors.text: Uses must scan every earlier assignment of the source variable
distractors.rationale: That scan is what multiple definitions forced.

distractors.text: The lexer records a unique token for each assignment
distractors.rationale: This is IR naming, not tokens.

distractors.text: Three-address already forbade reusing any temporary
distractors.rationale: Three-address still allows `x = 1; x = 2`. SSA is the extra rule.

quiz.correctExplanation: One def, so the use-def edge is unique. Walks replace reaching-definition searches.
objectiveIds: Explain why a single definition per name turns use-def into a graph walk

quiz.stem: In `x1 = 1; x2 = 2; x3 = φ(x1, x2)`, how many times is `x3` defined?
quiz.correctAnswer: Once: the φ is the single write of `x3`

distractors.text: Twice, because `x1` and `x2` both write `x3`
distractors.rationale: Those are operands, not writes of `x3`.

distractors.text: Zero: φ is a comment the backend will ignore
distractors.rationale: φ is a real SSA definition at the join.

distractors.text: Once per source token named `x`
distractors.rationale: Source spelling is gone; SSA versions are the names.

quiz.correctExplanation: φ is one instruction that defines `x3`. Operands are other names, already defined.
objectiveIds: Rewrite assignments so each name is defined exactly once

lessons.title: Use-def as a graph walk
explanation: Walking a use to its unique definition is the reason SSA exists. Start from three-address that still reassigns: `x = 1; x = x + y; z = x`. After renaming, `x1 = 1; x2 = x1 + y; z1 = x2`. The use of `x2` in `z1` has one incoming edge. There is no second writer of `x2` to consider.

CMU 15-411 treats that uniqueness as the thing that turns dataflow into a graph problem. Copy propagation is 'replace this use with the name it copies'. Dead-name deletion is 'if this definition has no uses, drop it'. Constant folding follows the same edges: if both operands of `x2 = x1 + y` are already constants, the definition of `x2` becomes a constant and every use updates.

Joins are where the graph would otherwise fork. Two predecessors that assign `x` cannot both write `x3`. The φ `x3 = φ(x1, x2)` is the extra definition that keeps the single-assignment rule at the merge. LLVM LangRef makes that φ a first-class instruction, not a comment.

The graph is not free. You must pick names so every use is dominated by its definition, or the form is garbage. A use of `x2` in a block that can run without executing `x2 = ...` is ill-formed. Verification is a later lesson. Here the operational claim is smaller: one def per name, so the walk has one step.

Three-address without SSA still has temporaries, so motion is possible. What it lacks is a unique writer. Any pass that asks 'where did this `x` come from?' falls back to reaching definitions. SSA is the renaming that answers that question by construction.
lessons.example: `x = 1; if (c) x = 2; return x + 0;` becomes `x1 = 1; x2 = 2; x3 = φ(x1, x2); t = x3 + 0; return t`. A fold that sees `+ 0` rewrites `t` to `x3` by walking one use-def edge. It does not search for every store to `x`.
lessons.whyItMatters: Missed optimizations that 'should have seen the constant' are often a name with two writers. SSA is how you stop searching.

quiz.stem: After `x1 = 1; x2 = x1 + 0`, a copy/fold walk that follows use-def will:
quiz.correctAnswer: Replace uses of `x2` with `x1`, because `x2` has one defining add-of-zero

distractors.text: Scan every assignment of the source variable `x` in the function
distractors.rationale: The single definition of `x2` is the only writer to follow.

distractors.text: Refuse to fold because three-address forbids replacing names
distractors.rationale: Three-address plus SSA is exactly the form that makes replacement local.

distractors.text: Re-lex the characters `x + 0` from the original file
distractors.rationale: The walk is on IR names, not source characters.

quiz.correctExplanation: One def of `x2`. The walk replaces uses. No reaching-definition search.
objectiveIds: Explain why a single definition per name turns use-def into a graph walk

quiz.stem: Which fragment still has two writers of one SSA name and is therefore not SSA?
quiz.correctAnswer: `x1 = 1; x1 = x1 + y` reusing `x1` for the sum

distractors.text: `x1 = 1; x2 = x1 + y` with a fresh name for the sum
distractors.rationale: That is already SSA: one write per name.

distractors.text: `x1 = 1; x2 = 2; x3 = φ(x1, x2)` at a join
distractors.rationale: The φ is a single write of `x3`; operands are other names.

distractors.text: `t1 = a + b; t2 = t1 * c` as ordinary three-address
distractors.rationale: Each temporary is written once; this is already compatible with SSA.

quiz.correctExplanation: Reassignment of `x1` is two definitions. SSA would have named the sum `x2`.
objectiveIds: Rewrite assignments so each name is defined exactly once

quiz.stem: Reaching-definition search versus SSA use-def differs because:
quiz.correctAnswer: SSA makes the unique writer an edge; reaching defs must consider several writers

distractors.text: Both require scanning every assignment of the source variable
distractors.rationale: SSA is the renaming that removes that scan.

distractors.text: SSA forbids naming the result of an add at all
distractors.rationale: SSA names every result; it just names it once.

distractors.text: Reaching definitions run in the lexer before any IR exists
distractors.rationale: Both analyses run on IR, after three-address exists.

quiz.correctExplanation: Several writers force a search. One writer is an edge you can walk.
objectiveIds: Explain why a single definition per name turns use-def into a graph walk

lessons.title: The merge at the join
explanation: Join points in a CFG are where two names of one variable meet. SSA cannot let both predecessors write the same name. A φ sits at the start of the join block and records, per incoming edge, which predecessor's value arrives: `x3 = φ(x1, x2)`. `x3` is a new definition. Each operand is tied to an edge, not to a runtime call.

LLVM LangRef makes the correspondence explicit: the first operand comes from the first predecessor, the second from the second. If the then-block wrote `x2 = 2` and the else-block left `x1 = 1` alone, the join is `x3 = φ(x1, x2)` with those blocks as the two predecessors.

Placement is at the join, not in the middle of a block. A φ that floated down next to an add would read like a function named phi and would break the 'one entry' story: the merge has to happen before the block's body uses the name. The CFG tells you where the join is; the φ is how SSA names it.
lessons.example: Then-block: `x2 = 2`. Else-block: no extra write, so `x1` still holds 1. Join: `x3 = φ(x1, x2)`. A use after the join mentions `x3`, never a bare `x`.
lessons.whyItMatters: Without the φ, SSA would have to pick one predecessor's name and lie about the other path.

quiz.stem: Then writes `x2 = 2`, else leaves `x1 = 1`. The join should contain:
quiz.correctAnswer: `x3 = φ(x1, x2)`, one operand per incoming edge

distractors.text: `x1 = x2` in the join, overwriting the else path's name
distractors.rationale: That reassigns `x1` and drops the else value.

distractors.text: No φ, because SSA already forbids merges
distractors.rationale: φ exists so the merge is a single new definition.

distractors.text: A runtime call `x3 = phi(x1, x2)` inserted after the join's first add
distractors.rationale: φ is an IR merge at block start, not a call in the body.

quiz.correctExplanation: One new name, two operands, each tied to a predecessor edge.
objectiveIds: Place a φ at a join so one name records which predecessor's value arrives

quiz.stem: Predict the φ operands when the left predecessor defines `a1` and the right defines `a2`:
quiz.correctAnswer: `a3 = φ(a1, a2)` with `a1` from the left edge and `a2` from the right

distractors.text: `a3 = φ(a3, a3)` because the join defines `a3` twice
distractors.rationale: Operands are the incoming names, not the φ's own result.

distractors.text: `a1 = φ(a2)` with a single operand for both edges
distractors.rationale: Each predecessor supplies its own operand.

distractors.text: No operands; the CFG edge magically forwards the latest `a`
distractors.rationale: SSA names the choice. Edges do not pick a version by themselves.

quiz.correctExplanation: Two edges, two operands, one new name. That is the φ.
objectiveIds: Predict the φ operands for a variable assigned on two incoming edges

quiz.stem: Trace `x1 = 1; if (c) x2 = 2; use x` through SSA at the join:
quiz.correctAnswer: The join defines `x3 = φ(x1, x2)` and the use reads `x3`

distractors.text: The use still reads `x`, which both blocks wrote
distractors.rationale: Source `x` is gone; each write has a version.

distractors.text: The then-block's `x2` is rewritten to `x1` before the branch
distractors.rationale: That would destroy the then value on that path.

distractors.text: A φ is placed in the entry block, before `x` is assigned
distractors.rationale: The merge belongs at the join, after both predecessors.

quiz.correctExplanation: Entry writes `x1`, then writes `x2`, join writes `x3`. The use follows `x3`.
objectiveIds: Place a φ at a join so one name records which predecessor's value arrives

lessons.title: Promote the slot that stays home
explanation: Alloca slots look like memory even when they behave like locals. A front-end often emits `%x = alloca i32`, then `store` and `load` for every mention of `x`. Those loads hide the value from SSA: each load looks like a new def from memory. mem2reg promotes an alloca that never escapes into an SSA name, replacing loads and stores with versions and φs.

Never escapes means the address is not stored, not passed to another function, not returned. The slot is a private local. Then `store 1, %x` becomes `x1 = 1`, a later `store 2` on the other path becomes `x2 = 2`, and the join load becomes `x3 = φ(x1, x2)`. LLVM's mem2reg pass is this promotion.

Some slots must stay in memory. The address is taken and given to a callee. The slot is volatile. Two pointers might alias it. Promotion would invent a register the rest of the program can still reach through a pointer. Those stay as loads and stores.
lessons.example: `%a = alloca i32; store 1, %a; if (c) store 2, %a; %r = load %a` with no other use of `%a` becomes `x1 = 1; x2 = 2; x3 = φ(x1, x2)`. If the body also does `call f(%a)`, the address escaped and the alloca stays.
lessons.whyItMatters: SSA cannot see through memory. Promoting the local is how `-O1` suddenly looks like a different language.

quiz.stem: Promote `%x = alloca i32; store 1, %x; %r = load %x` when `%x` does not escape:
quiz.correctAnswer: `x1 = 1` and `%r` rewritten to use `x1`, alloca removed

distractors.text: Keep the load and store; SSA already sees through memory
distractors.rationale: Loads hide the value; promotion is what exposes it.

distractors.text: Replace the alloca with a heap object the callee can share
distractors.rationale: Promotion goes to an SSA value, not to the heap.

distractors.text: Delete the store and leave `%r` as an uninitialized name
distractors.rationale: The store's value is the new SSA definition, not dead.

quiz.correctExplanation: The store becomes a def, the load becomes a use of that def, the slot goes away.
objectiveIds: Promote an alloca that never escapes into an SSA value

quiz.stem: A stack slot must stay in memory when:
quiz.correctAnswer: Its address is passed to a callee, so the slot escapes

distractors.text: It is assigned more than once in the source function
distractors.rationale: Multiple assignments become φs after promotion; they do not force memory.

distractors.text: SSA form is in use anywhere in the module
distractors.rationale: SSA is the destination of promotion, not a reason to refuse it.

distractors.text: The slot holds an integer rather than a pointer
distractors.rationale: Type is not the escape test; taking the address is.

quiz.correctExplanation: Escape means someone else can load through a pointer. That slot is really memory.
objectiveIds: Name a reason a stack slot must stay in memory instead of becoming a register

quiz.stem: After promoting a non-escaping alloca assigned on two incoming edges, the join holds:
quiz.correctAnswer: A φ of the two stored values, in place of the join load

distractors.text: The original load, because φ cannot replace memory
distractors.rationale: Replacing that load is the point of mem2reg.

distractors.text: Two remaining stores and no SSA names
distractors.rationale: The stores become the φ's operands.

distractors.text: A call to a runtime helper named mem2reg
distractors.rationale: mem2reg is a compile-time rewrite, not a call.

quiz.correctExplanation: Each path's store becomes a version; the load at the join becomes the φ.
objectiveIds: Promote an alloca that never escapes into an SSA value

lessons.title: Well-formed or rejected
explanation: Types and dominance are a contract the IR verifier checks, not a hope. Every use of a name must be dominated by that name's definition: every path to the use has already executed the write. The types on operands must match the operator. LLVM LangRef writes this as well-formedness. A pass that breaks it has a bug, even if the generated code happened to work once.

A classic ill-formed fragment: `x2` is defined in the then-block, then used in a join that also has an else-path that never defined `x2`. The use is not dominated. The repair is a φ at the join, or not using `x2` there. Another: `x3 = φ(x1, x2)` where `x1` is i32 and `x2` is i64. Types do not agree.

Verification is cheap compared with debugging a later pass that assumed the contract. Run it after every transform that mints names or moves uses. A φ that is not at the start of its block, a use that floats above its def, a binary add of a pointer and a token-like opaque type: those are verifier rejections, not optimizer opinions.
lessons.example: Then-block defines `x2 = 2`. Join uses `x2` directly on the else path as well. The verifier rejects: the else path reaches the use without the def. Legal form is `x3 = φ(x1, x2)` with `x1` defined on the else path.
lessons.whyItMatters: An optimizer that trusts broken SSA will propagate a value that was never written on that path. The verifier is the cheap alarm.

quiz.stem: Every SSA use must be dominated by its definition, meaning:
quiz.correctAnswer: Every path to the use has already executed that unique write

distractors.text: Some path to the use executed the write, even if another did not
distractors.rationale: Dominance requires all paths, not one.

distractors.text: The use appears earlier in the instruction dump than the write
distractors.rationale: Textual order is not dominance; CFG paths are.

distractors.text: The lexer listed the name before any assignment in the file
distractors.rationale: Dominance is an IR CFG fact, not a source-token fact.

quiz.correctExplanation: All paths, that one write. That is the dominance half of well-formed SSA.
objectiveIds: Check that every use is dominated by its definition and that types agree

quiz.stem: Which fragment should the verifier reject?
quiz.correctAnswer: A join that uses `x2` defined only in the then-block, with no φ

distractors.text: `x3 = φ(x1, x2)` at the join with matching types and dominated operands
distractors.rationale: That is the well-formed repair.

distractors.text: `t1 = a + b` in a block that dominates its only use
distractors.rationale: Dominated use, matching types: well-formed.

distractors.text: A three-address add whose result is named once and used later in the same block
distractors.rationale: Same-block later uses are dominated by construction.

quiz.correctExplanation: The else path reaches the use with no def of `x2`. That is ill-formed SSA.

quiz.stem: `x3 = φ(x1, x2)` with `x1` i32 and `x2` i64 is rejected because:
quiz.correctAnswer: The φ operands' types do not agree with each other

distractors.text: φ nodes are illegal once three-address exists
distractors.rationale: φ is how SSA merges three-address names.

distractors.text: Dominance failed: `x3` is used in its own operand list
distractors.rationale: The bug here is types, not a self-use.

distractors.text: i32 and i64 are the same type after lowering
distractors.rationale: They are different widths; the verifier cares.

quiz.correctExplanation: Types must agree. A mixed-width φ is ill-formed even if dominance holds.
objectiveIds: Check that every use is dominated by its definition and that types agree
